subject: toucan
pitch: A keel-billed toucan showing off on a short mossy branch. A huge rainbow beak in lime green, sky blue and orange with a cherry-red tip, a glossy black body, a lemon-yellow bib, a ring of lime-green skin around each eye, bright blue feet and a scarlet patch under the tail. A single pink orchid blooms on the branch beside it.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module using the SDK for a toucan scene on a mossy branch with an orchid, thinking through realistic proportions for a keel-billed toucan including its body and distinctive beak length.

The model faces +Z with the branch resting on the ground and the bird perched above it, feet contacting the branch around 0.12m up. I'm deciding which SDK functions to import and planning the beak as a sweep shape with colored bands—lime green, sky blue, orange, and cherry-red—to capture the toucan's signature rainbow beak, using a loft for its tall cross-section.

Now I'm sketching the overall proportions: branch running along Z under the bird, bird body centered around 0.42m up, with total length near 0.5m from beak tip to tail. I'm starting to lay out the spine skeleton as a catmull chain from the hips through the chest.

I'm mapping the tail chain hanging downward from the hips, the neck chain rising to the head joint, and deciding to keep the implementation reasonably simple — body sweep with color bands, head sweep, beak, eye rings, feet, wing membranes, tail with a red patch, an orchid built from petal lathes, moss cards on the branch, and the branch itself as a painted sweep — then beginning to define the joint hierarchy starting with the hips root.

Writing joint chains...

Now I'm working out the beak geometry: a curved bezier path from base to tip with a tapering radius that's tall and narrow at the base, shrinking toward a pointed tip, colored with bands transitioning from lime green at the base through sky blue and orange to a cherry-red tip, matching the keel-billed toucan's distinctive coloring.

I'm adding a separate jaw joint beneath the head so the lower mandible can open independently, giving it its own smaller sweep with a similar but subtler color gradient. For the eyes, I'm planning a dark iris sphere surrounded by a thin ring of lime-green skin built from a closed tube sweep along a circular path around each eye socket.

Now I'm working out eye placement using the head's local coordinate system, deciding whether to use left/right/forward/up conventions or find the nearest surface point on the head sweep so the eye spheres sit flush against the head's curved surface rather than floating.

I realize a flat ring placed in the tangent plane would float slightly off the curved surface, so instead I'm planning to drape a closed circular path onto the head surface with a small lift offset, generating the loop points as a circle of radius 0.035 around the eye position.

For the eye itself, I'll use a small dark sphere embedded partway into the head surface near the beak base, positioning it symmetrically on either side of the head's center. Then I'm moving on to the black glossy body, planning a sweep along the spine chain with a varying radius for the chest bulk.

Still writing body radius function...

Actually I'll use a paint function keyed off position to color the bib yellow on the chest, the undertail red near the tail base, and black everywhere else, using normal and position thresholds for hard faceted edges.

For the tail, I'm sweeping a catmull-rom chain from the hips down and back through several joints, tapering the cross-section so it's flat dorsoventrally, then coloring it black — the red undertail patch is already handled by the body paint near the hip base.

Now I'm figuring out the folded wings, deciding between a simple sweep along a shoulder-to-tip path or an extruded 2D silhouette in the side plane, leaning toward the extrusion approach with an outline shape placed against the body side for a more convincing folded-wing look.

Now I'm working out the leg placement for feet standing on the branch, checking that hip-to-foot distances stay within reach of the two-segment limb lengths. I settle on hip joints around y=0.36 with thigh/shin lengths of 0.14 and 0.12, targeting feet near the branch surface at y≈0.112, verifying the geometry stays just within range without being fully straight.

For the leg chain, I name the three limb points hipL/kneeL/ankleL so the tip becomes a proper foot joint, then plan to add zygodactyl toes (two forward, two back) as simple sweeps extending from each foot tip frame.

I'll give each foot four zygodactyl toes as small two-point sweeps, nudging the toe height to about 0.107 so they hug the branch surface instead of floating.

For the branch itself, I'm sweeping a gently curved catmull-rom path at ground level, sized so it just touches the floor, and keeping it short (roughly z -0.7 to 0.7) relative to the bird's body and tail span.

I'm thinking through how to paint the branch convincingly: a bark color overall, but switching to a mottled moss green wherever the surface normal points upward enough, using a paint function that can nest another paint call for the mottling effect, and considering whether to add scattered moss detail on top of that base texture.

Now I'm working out the moss clumps as small flattened spheres stuck onto the branch surface, randomly distributed with a seeded RNG for consistency, and then designing a pink orchid growing from the branch beside the bird — sprouting a thin stem upward from a point on the branch surface to a bloom position, then arranging five petals radially around the flower head using angular offsets.

Working through petal orientation math...

Now I'm thinking about attaching the petal at point F, and planning the orchid's lip and stem structure—using a small sphere for the central lip, then sprouting the stem with a curved catmull path going upward from the hit point.

I'm figuring out the orchid's flower head position at the tip point and double-checking it doesn't collide with the bird's body or feet, since both are near the branch at similar coordinates. I'm considering shifting the orchid further out in x and z to keep it clearly beside the perched bird rather than overlapping it.

Actually the branch curves slightly with x near zero throughout, so placing the orchid off-center at x=-0.12 would float off the branch surface. I need the orchid to sit where the branch actually is, but that spot risks colliding with the tail—so I'm reconsidering a front-right position near z=0.45, below the beak and in front of the chest, away from feet, as a cleaner "beside the bird" placement.

I'll finalize the branch path so it bends gently leftward toward the front, letting it dip to around x=-0.08 to -0.14 by z=0.42-0.7, placing the orchid near (-0.08, 0.12, 0.42) with its stem rising just below the beak's reach—clear of the bird's face and tail, resting naturally on the curved branch.

Now I'm setting up the toucan's spine as a catmull curve from hips through chest to neck, with joints sitting at each span's start point, and planning the head joint to parent off the final spine segment.

For the body mesh I'm using a sweep along that spine chain, tapering the radius down near the head so the neck transitions smoothly into a separate head sweep.

I'm defining a radius function that returns [rx, ry] widths at each point along the body, interpolated between a set of key positions from hips to head, then sketching a small bezier path for the head's own sweep geometry with its own radius taper.

For coloring, I'm setting up paint rules based on each point's position and normal: black for the head, yellow for a throat bib where z is high and y is low enough, red for the undertail region near the bottom and back, and I'm planning a separate lime-green ring around the eyes to match the keel-billed toucan's distinctive bare skin patch.

Now I'm shaping the massive stylized beak as a curved bone structure using a cubic bezier path running upward and forward from the face, tapering in radius toward the tip, with colored bands transitioning from lime at the base through sky blue, orange, and red toward the point. I'm also starting the lower mandible as a separate jaw bone with its own downward-curving bezier path beneath the upper beak.

I'm deciding whether to rig a proper jaw joint for articulation, concluding yes for flexibility. Next I'm planning the skin ring around the eyes and then moving to legs and feet, using dark grey/black tube sweeps for the legs and bright blue for the toes, structured as a joint chain running from hip through knee to ankle.

I'm working out leg placement using inverse kinematics, checking that the hip-to-ankle distance stays within the bone length limits so the leg bends naturally rather than locking straight, adjusting root and target positions and segment lengths until the geometry reaches comfortably with a slight knee bend.

Now I'm planning the feet: dark grey legs, and four zygodactyl toes per foot (two pointing forward, two back) built as thin swept polylines branching from the ankle joint position.

For the toe segments, I'll switch to capsule primitives connecting two points with a small radius, attaching each to the foot's tip joint, and skip claws for simplicity since I need a reliable fallback if the tip joint is null.

Next I'm setting up the tail as a chain from the hips following a curved catmull-rom path with a tapering radius, colored to match the plumage.

Now I'm defining the wing geometry, extruding it from a spine joint, positioning it against the body's outer surface in black, and working out the outline points for its shape relative to the attachment position.

I'm also noting that since the extrusion's thickness axis cancels across the X-direction, I can mirror the wing simply by changing the "at" position for each side. Now I'm picking the colour palette for the toucan—black, lemon yellow for the bib, lime green, sky blue, and orange accents.

Finishing the colour list with cherry red, blue for the feet, grey for the legs, bark brown, moss greens, pinks, stem green, and a dark eye tone, keeping the flat colour count under the limit. Then I'm working out how to place an eye ring on the head surface by sampling the sweep mesh and generating a circular set of points via trigonometry, draping a closed Catmull-Rom path onto the head surface with a slight lift, and sweeping a thin tube along it to form the ring in lime color.

Still writing eye and scatter logic...

I'm working out paint logic for the branch surface, using a conditional mottled texture for mossy areas versus plain bark elsewhere. Then I'm starting to extrude petal shapes at the flower tip, positioning each petal's outline relative to its base.

Still writing petal geometry...

I'm also setting up the radial spacing for five petals around the stem, planning colors, and placing the lip and center with small sphere accents using directional frames. Lime green skin rings and bright blue feet are confirmed as handled already, so I'm moving on to work out the scarlet underside details.

For the rig structure I'm defining role labels for head, jaw, spine, tail, and leg chains so each joint can be referenced properly, then exporting the final builder with name and description metadata. I'm also checking that the body surface sweep correctly maps t-values across the spine chain so proportions stay consistent along its length.

Now I'm writing a helper function that interpolates radius values between keyframes along the body, beak, and head to get smooth tapering shapes, defining typed tuples for each radius profile so TypeScript doesn't complain about the return shape.

I'm setting up the lower mandible's radius keyframes and color bands matching the toucan's lime/sky/orange/red palette, then building the plumage sweep along the spine chain and defining the head joint's position and aim direction relative to the spine.

Now I'm placing the jaw joint and working out the branch geometry — a catmull-rom path with constant radius and rounded end caps, checking that the branch bottom sits flush at y=0 and spans the right z-range.

I shorten the branch path and check that the orchid, moss scatter, and toucan's feet/tail don't collide with it. For the feet, I define toe offsets as small capsules branching from each leg's tip joint, using paired radius tapers for the leg sweep.

Then I work through the orchid: defining a typed petal outline array, looping five extrusions radially around a tip point with tapered thickness and bevel, and adding a sphere-stick lip for the flower center. I settle on imports needed from the builder library (THREE, frame, limb, mottle, paint, rng, bezier, catmull, OutlinePoint type) and start defining the color palette as hex constants for plumage, bark, moss, and orchid parts.

I draft a paint function for the toucan's plumage that assigns yellow, red, or black based on position and normal direction, then a mottled bark paint for the branch. I lay out the builder calls step by step — sweeping the branch path, scattering moss sphere-sticks across its upper surface, then building the spine as a chain of named joints (hips, back, chest, neck) acting as the root, followed by a tapered body sweep using keyed radius profiles. I continue into the head joint and skull sweep, then the jaw joint and upper beak curve using a bezier path with tapering radius.

I shift to finishing the beak with a banded color sweep (lime to sky to orange to red) along its length, then the lower mandible sweep, being careful that the beak origin sits inside the head sweep to avoid gaps. I work out the eye geometry by taking nearest-surface hits on the skull for each side, generating a ring of points via a circular loop projected locally, draping that ring back onto the head surface for an eye-ring sweep, and adding a small sphere-stick for the eyeball itself, checking distances to confirm the hit points land close to the sweep surface.

Next I build the tail as a chain parented to the hip joint, sweep it with a tapered radius, and reuse the plumage paint so a red patch appears on the tail's underside near the body junction, restricting the z-range so it reads as a believable undertail patch rather than covering the whole tail. I sketch a wing outline with a sharp point at the wingtip, extruding it on both sides of the body at the back spine joint with a tapered thickness.

For the legs, I use a limb() call to generate joint points from hip to ankle with a bend direction, build a chain with named hip/knee/ankle joints parented to the hips, sweep it with a tapered leg radius, then attach four toe capsules as offsets from the ankle tip joint, each colored for the foot. I finish with the orchid: finding a surface hit on the branch for the stem base, sprouting a thin stem to a tip point, extruding the five petals around that tip, and adding a sphere-stick lip, then returning the builder's root as the final output while double-checking joint ordering, typing of tuples, and that all referenced bones exist before being used.
